title: Designing Reliable Power
summary: Use redundancy and backup concepts to reason about a power design without performing electrical work.
objectives: Explain why a critical system should not depend on one path.
Compare a single power path with a conceptual primary-and-backup design.

vocab.def: An additional path or component available if another one fails.
One part whose failure can stop the larger system.
The ability of a system to keep performing as expected over time.

sections.heading: Plan for interruptions
sections.body: Computing equipment depends on power. A design can include a primary supply, backup systems, and monitoring so a team has more than one way to respond to an interruption.

sections.heading: One path or more than one
sections.body: If one path is the only path, it is a single point of failure. A primary path plus an independent backup can improve resilience, though it adds resources and complexity.

sections.heading: Design on paper
sections.body: Draw two conceptual power paths to a server and label the backup. Do not wire circuits, open panels, service generators, or touch mains electricity. Those tasks require qualified professionals.

practice.prompt: Compare a design with one power path to one with a primary and backup path. What reliability benefit and resource tradeoff does the second design have?

quiz.question: What does redundancy provide?
options: Another available path or component if one fails
A guarantee that nothing can fail
quiz.answer: Another available path or component if one fails

reflectionPrompt: Where might adding a backup improve a design, and what resource might that require?
